articles.title: India to Replace Russian Fregat Radar Parts With Local Systems in Talwar-Class
articles.text:
The Indian Navy is pursuing a sustained component-level indagenisation effort for the Russian Fregat M2EM air-search radar. The latest tender from them (GEM/2026/B/7860465) is seeking indigenous development of a flexible waveguide section used by the system.
The new procurement request was issued by the Indian Navy for work at Weapon and Electronics Certification and Reliability Services (WECORS), Naval Dockyard Mumbai. The requirement covers indigenous development of Fregat M2EM’s waveguide flexible section (with reference to the Russian drawing/part number ЛП2.060.173).
The tender, published on September 4, 2026, closes on September 25. It is a single item development requirement, and carries an EMD of Rs78,500. The use of the original Russian part reference demonstrates the nature of the Navy’s effort: rather than just sourcing replacement components, Indian industry is being asked to develop domestic alternatives for the individual elements of the radar.
The Fregat M2EM radar is the three-dimensional air-search radar associated with India’s Russian-built Talwar class (Project 1135.6) frigates. The ships also employ the Shtil surface-to-air missile system. In August 2026, the Navy issued GEM/2026/B/7901493 for indigenisation of the Channel 2 mixer and amplifier associated with Fregat M2EM. Another requirement (GEM/2026/R/705884) issued in July, sought indigenous design and development of the Channel 1 mixer and amplifier.
The Navy has been procuring repair capability for defective Fregat M2EM (and Shtil system) modules. A July 2026 tender from the Weapon Equipment Depot at Naval Dockyard Mumbai covered repair to defective radar and missile-system modules. In April 2024 the Navy floated a rate contract for the repair and refurbishment of Fregat waveguides. The contract was subsequently awarded to Indian firms, including Niyura Technologies.
That progression — from repair and refurbishment to component development and manufacture — is significant for the sustainment of older Russian-origin systems. The individual GeM requirements are relatively small in contrast with major naval acquisition programmes. But they nevertheless have more consequence.
Fregat radar mixers, amplifiers, waveguides and electronic modules are being addressed individually, while separate repair contracts ensure that existing equipment is kept serviceable. The approach also demonstrates how indigenisation can be pursued without waiting for a major replacement programme. For ships that are going to be in commission for years, creating Indian sources for critical components can help reduce reliance on foreign spares and improve long-term maintainability.
Edited By Raunak Kunde

articles.title: Indian INSAS 1B1 Rifle Spotted With Taliban in Afghanistan
articles.text:
An Indian-made INSAS 1B1 assault rifle turned up in the hands of the Taliban in Afghanistan, prompting questions about how the guns got there. The rifle was identified from video images on the internet. It resembles the INSAS 1B1 assault rifle, an upgraded version of the INSAS, which was issued to Indian troops. According to government documents, the Rifle 1B1 was issued to Indian soldiers in 2001, after upgrades were made to its original design. The rifle in the images seems to have the black synthetic furniture of the improved rifle, rather than the orange brown polymer or wooden furniture of the original INSAS rifles.
The rifle in the video also uses the translucent polymer magazine, typical of the INSAS rifles. It can be difficult to identify the exact variant of the rifle in video images.
The Indian government has acknowledged that the INSAS rifles were in service in the 1990s, and later modified to address deficiencies. There is no official documentation that INSAS rifles were sold to the Afghan government, or that they were transferred to the Taliban.
India has provided military assistance to Afghanistan, but the mere presence of an Indian rifle in the hands of the Taliban is not enough to prove that it was supplied by India.
This is an important distinction, since weapons often change hands on battlefields, and are sometimes sold, transferred, stolen, or smuggled across borders. Defense analysts speculate that it may have been stolen from Indian military warehouses, and sold through black markets in the region. Another possibility is that an Indian-made rifle, stolen, purchased, or captured by Pakistani militants in Jammu and Kashmir, was smuggled into Afghanistan.
There is no official documentation that this might have happened. It is possible that an undocumented supply of INSAS rifles may have occurred recently. It is also impossible to say, from the video images alone, whether it is a 1B1 or another variant of the rifle.
The sighting of an INSAS 1B1 rifle in the hands of the Taliban is more of a mystery than anything else. The rifle seems to be a later model, which would suggest that it was supplied to the Taliban somehow, rather than being captured from Afghan government stocks. The serial number would have to be examined to identify which Indian unit, if any, originally owned the rifle, when it was issued, and how it may have gotten to Afghanistan.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

articles.title: Desan Shipyard Launches First MPMS for Malaysian Coast Guard in Istanbul
articles.text:
The Malaysian Maritime Agency (Maritim Malaysia) has achieved another significant milestone through the launch of the Multi Purpose Mission Ship (MPMS 1) at the Desan Shipyard in Türkiye yesterday.

Malaysian Maritime Agency press release

The launch ceremony was attended by the Minister of Home Affairs, the Honorable Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution bin Ismail, along with the Minister of Home Affairs of Türkiye, His Excellency Mustafa Çiftçi, and the Minister of Industry and Technology of Türkiye, His Excellency Mehmet Fatih Kacır, as well as delegations from both countries.

The MPMS 1 construction marks a significant advancement in the development of strategic assets, expanding the scope of operations and strengthening Malaysia’s maritime presence in the sea. As a multi-purpose ship, MPMS 1 is designed to perform maritime surveillance, search and rescue operations (CARILAMAT), humanitarian assistance, disaster response, and various other operational needs.

The Director General of Maritim Malaysia, Laksamana Maritim Datuk Haji Mohd Rosli bin Abdullah, said the MPMS 1 is a capability multiplier that will enhance Malaysia’s maritime operational resilience in the face of increasingly complex maritime security challenges.

“This capability is a more effective way to ensure operations. Our focus is to ensure that this new capability is fully utilized to safeguard the country’s security, sovereignty, and interests in the Maritime Zone,” he said.

The construction of MPMS 1 has reached approximately 85 percent and is ahead of schedule. Meanwhile, the construction of MPMS 2 has reached 34.05 percent, compared to the planned 32 percent, indicating positive progress in the efforts to strengthen Malaysia’s maritime capabilities on a phased basis.

MPMS 1 is expected to be brought back to Malaysia in early 2027 and is planned to join the Langkawi International Maritime and Aerospace Exhibition (LIMA) 2027 to introduce the agency’s new capabilities to the public and the international maritime community.

The MPMS project also reflects Malaysia-Turkey’s strategic relationship in the maritime industry, in addition to opening up broader cooperation between Malaysia’s Maritime and Coast Guard and the Turkish Coast Guard in the field of training, capacity building, CARILAMAT, information sharing, and joint exercises.

The event was also attended by the Deputy Director General of Maritime Logistics Malaysia, Lieutenant Admiral Maritim Datuk Saiful Lizan bin Ibrahim, senior officers from the Ministry of Home Affairs, Malaysia Maritime and the Ministry of Economy, the Malaysian Ambassador to the Republic of Türkiye, and the Consul General in Istanbul, as well as agency representatives and stakeholders directly involved in the shipbuilding project. The event was also attended by representatives from the Government of the Republic of Türkiye and the management team of Desan Shipyard.

The launch of MPMS 1 is a concrete step towards forming a more modern, resilient, and responsive Malaysian maritime fleet to protect the people, preserve maritime resources, and safeguard national interests, in line with the mandate to Control, Protect, and Rescue.

articles.title: India Could Seal MRFA Deal by FY-End, Says IAF Chief
articles.text:
India is looking at finalising the much-awaited multi-role fighter aircraft (MRFA) deal by this financial year provided things go as per plan, Chief of Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal A P Singh, said on Saturday.
In its largest-ever defence acquisition push, India in February cleared a long-pending proposal to procure 114 Rafale fighter jets under a government-to-government framework with France, nearly two decades after the plan was originally rolled out to boost the Indian Air Force’s combat prowess.
The price negotiations and other critical issues relating to the project are currently underway.
Addressing a press conference ahead of Air Force Day, the Air Chief Marshal also said that the force may have to look at the procurement of another platform if the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) programme faces delays.
“Russia has offered us Su-57 jets, but no decision has been made on it,” he said.
Responding to a question on the depleting strength of fighter squadrons, Air Chief Marshal Singh said the Indian Air Force (IAF) needs at least 36 to 40 aircraft annually in the next few years.
He said air power remains crucial in the context of overall military strength and that India needs to further ramp up its air power.
On modernisation of the IAF, he said the force has to be augmented through artificial intelligence
“We have to have an AI-augmented force,” he said.
Self-reliance is crucial for overall combat readiness, he added.
The Chief of Air Staff also underlined the need for India to produce a fighter jet engine in the country. PTI

AMCA By 2028 ‘Impossible’, Says Geo-Political Analyst Mitra
articles.text:
India’s target for the first flight of the prototype of its Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) by September 2028 was questioned by strategic affairs writer Abhijit Iyer-Mitra, who said that the programme still has a number of critical development milestones to clear before an aircraft can safely enter flight testing.
Speaking to The Times of India in the Defence Expresso programme, Iyer-Mitra said the proposed timeline was not realistic, given that the private-sector developer of the AMCA had not yet been selected and that the contract had not yet been awarded. Iyer-Mitra’s main argument was that first flight cannot simply be thought of as the next step after choosing a manufacturer.
He said that the successful private-sector consortium would first need to work through the aircraft’s detailed design and systems architecture before a prototype could be built. According to him it would be realistic to have a design freeze by around 2030, followed by prototype development and subsequent flight testing.
He also questioned if the requirements for the current AMCA would change during development, given that developments in warfare could see changes in the fifth-generation threats, and the experience of the use of drones so far could see changes to the aircraft’s requirements before the design freeze. He argued that producing an airworthy prototype was only one stage, with extensive testing required afterwards for the aircraft’s flight-control systems, avionics, propulsion, weapons integration and redundancy architecture.
He particularly stressed on systems integration, arguing that an aircraft’s performance cannot be judged based on such headline specifications as speed, range, thrust or lift, but that the interaction between the numerous subsystems has to be validated before the aircraft can enter an extensive flight-test programme.
This is particularly important for AMCA, because the programme has the goal of producing a fifth-generation fighter rather than just another conventional fighter airframe. Iyer-Mitra was in support of handing the AMCA development to India’s private sector, but cautioned against unrealistic schedules imposed on the selected company.
The government has shortlisted private-sector led consortia for the programme, and Iyer-Mitra argued that the selected developer would need sufficient time to set up the design, systems-integration architecture and production approach.
He warned that companies would be tempted to submit aggressive timelines in the bidding process, because shorter schedules would look more attractive for bidders. According to him, this could lead to a situation where the realistic development schedule would be punished during the evaluation.
The interview also looked into the propulsion requirement of the AMCA. Iyer-Mitra spoke about several possible foreign technology partnerships, and argued that the eventual objective should be to develop greater Indian capability and intellectual property around the engine. He suggested that even a later first flight could leave India with a viable fifth-generation fighter programme, provided that the resulting aircraft was well-designed and supported by the industrial ecosystem that would be necessary for it.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

articles.title: Sanjay Kumar named Petronet LNG’s next CEO
articles.text: Sanjay Kumar, Director (Marketing) at state-owned GAIL (India) Ltd, has been named the next Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Petronet LNG Ltd. His term will begin on May 13, 2027, following the conclusion of current CEO A K Singh's extended tenure.Petronet's board finalized the decision during a 15-minute meeting on October 2, as disclosed in a regulatory filing. Kumar, 59, has been appointed for a five-year tenure.Also read: India's crude imports hit 2026 high in September as Gulf supplies surge despite Hormuz risksAs India's largest liquefied natural gas importer, Petronet is majority-owned by state-run energy companies, with Indian Oil Corporation (IOC), GAIL (India) Ltd, Oil and Natural Gas Corp (ONGC), and Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd (BPCL) each holding a 12.5% stake. Although chaired by the Union Petroleum Secretary, Petronet is registered as a private limited entity. Consequently, it operates outside the jurisdiction of government watchdogs such as the CAG, CVC, and RTI. Board executives are subject to a retirement age of 65, compared to 60 at public sector units, and receive higher compensation than PSU counterparts.Kumar, who has served as GAIL's Marketing Director since mid-June 2023, holds a mechanical engineering degree from IIT Kharagpur and an MBA. He brings more than 35 years of industry experience across the natural gas and LNG value chain.Petronet LNG manages India's premier LNG import facility at Dahej in Gujarat alongside a second terminal at Kochi in Kerala. Together, these facilities offer a combined regasification capacity of 27.5 million tonnes per annum (MMTPA) - 22.5 MMTPA at Dahej and 5 MMTPA at Kochi. The company manages roughly 74% of the nation's LNG imports and fulfills about 34% of overall gas consumption.Also read: G7 nations agree to release 100 million barrels of oil, including diesel, a boost for TrumpThis leadership change coincides with national efforts to boost natural gas within the energy mix and expand gas infrastructure. To support these goals, Petronet is advancing plans to increase Dahej's regasification capacity, build a greenfield LNG facility on the east coast, and construct a petrochemical project at Dahej.

articles.title: US Indo-Pacific Command Chief in India to Deepen Military Cooperation
articles.text:
Admiral Samuel J. Paparo, Commander of the US Indo-Pacific Command, is visiting India, starting Saturday, to advance defence ties and military-to-military cooperation, the US Embassy in India said.
Sharing the details of his visit, the US mission said, “During his visit, Admiral Paparo will engage with Indian counterparts on shared security priorities, including harnessing digital transformation and emerging technologies, maintaining regional strategic stability, strengthening defence energy resilience, and navigating an increasingly competitive technology landscape.”
According to the US Embassy, both nations are building a defence partnership equipped to meet the challenges of the future — from emerging technology to maritime security.
“Admiral Paparo’s visit underscores the strength of the Major Defence Partnership and reaffirms the United States’ enduring presence and interests in the Indian Ocean region,” it added.
Admiral Paparo last visited India from February 14–19 earlier this year. That visit reinforced bilateral defence ties and strategic security cooperation.
He met with then Chief of Defence Staff General Anil Chauhan and then Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Dinesh Kumar Tripathi in New Delhi to discuss regional maritime security and joint operational capabilities.
He also visited the Indian Army’s Western Command headquarters in Haryana’s Chandimandir alongside US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor for operational briefings with Lt. Gen. Manoj Kumar Katiyar.
Admiral Paparo then visited Bengaluru and toured the National Flight Test Centre to inspect aerospace innovation and HAL Tejas facilities, emphasising expanding technology partnerships.
India-US defence cooperation is a comprehensive major partnership built on foundational logistics pacts, joint military exercises, and co-production of advanced military technology in the Indo-Pacific.
According to an expert assessment presented at the US Army Command and General Staff College, US-India defence ties are “really strong and growing”.
India and the United States have significantly expanded defence cooperation over the past two decades, including through more frequent military exercises, defence technology initiatives and agreements intended to improve military interoperability.
India is also a member of the Quad alongside the United States, Japan and Australia. New Delhi has simultaneously maintained its emphasis on strategic autonomy and its participation in BRICS, reflecting its approach of pursuing relationships with multiple major powers rather than entering a formal US-led alliance.

articles.title: Former US Intelligence Officer Recalls Surprise Over India’s ASAT Test
articles.text:
US Air Force intelligence officer (retired) David Grusch has related the reaction of the United States to the news of India’s 2019 anti-satellite (ASAT) test. In his interview on The Joe Rogan Experience, Grusch revealed that the unexpected destruction of an Indian satellite has caused US intelligence officers to investigate the resulting debris field.
Speaking to Joe Rogan, Grusch stated that he was on duty within the US National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) Operations Center when India executed what would become known as Mission Shakti on March 27, 2019. According to his account, the US government became aware of India’s action but was surprised when it became clear that India had chosen to intercept its own satellite.
Grusch said that NRO became worried about the debris because American reconnaissance satellites are operating in space. He recalled that he contacted officials while the orbital analysts worked to calculate the debris field and assess the risk for US spacecraft that had to perform any manoeuvres.
This gives a first-hand account of the US intelligence response, but Grusch’s account should be taken in context as his recollection of events, rather than an official view from the US government. India announced Mission Shakti after successfully intercepting Microsat-R, an Indian satellite, using a ground-launched interceptor that had been developed by DRDO. The government stated that it demonstrated an indigenous capability to intercept a satellite in low-Earth orbit.
The low altitude was essential to India’s argument for the test. The Ministry of External Affairs said that the interception was executed in the lower atmosphere to reduce the duration of the debris in orbit, with the fragments expected to decay and fall back to Earth within weeks. Nevertheless, Ministry of External Affairs US military sensors tracked hundreds of fragments of debris following the interception.
Contemporary reports said that the US military was tracking at least 270 pieces and ready to warn satellite operators in the event of a potential collision. DRDO chief G. Satheesh Reddy said in May 2019 that most of the debris had already decayed, and the remaining fragments were expected to dissipate within a short period. The Indian Express NASA, on the other hand, reported that some fragments had reached higher apogees and temporarily increased the risk for spacecraft, including the International Space Station.
NASA Administrator Jim Bridenstine said that the risk to the ISS from small debris impacts had increased throughout the period immediately following the test. Mission Shakti has made India the fourth country, following the United States, Russia and China, to publicly demonstrate a kinetic ASAT. The test also demonstrated India’s ability to use a ballistic missile defence-derived interceptor against a satellite in orbit.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

DRDO Develops Portable Sonar to Detect Underwater Divers
articles.text:
The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has developed the new Portable Diver Detection Sonar (PDDS-X) for the detection, tracking and classification of possible underwater threats like divers and other targets in shallow water areas. The sonar comprises an underwater unit and a shore unit that are connected together.
The underwater component can be placed in various locations including alongside a harbour wall, on a pier or on the seabed to meet specific requirements. It uses acoustic sensing to monitor and detect potential targets in the nearby water environment.
Its role is to provide detection, tracking and classification, rather than simply an alert when an object has entered a monitored area. One of the stated features of PDDS-X is the ability to detect targets in 360 degrees in azimuth. This is important since it provides protection around the deployed underwater sensor, covering all directions rather than one direction only.
This could be useful in protecting fixed locations when threats could come from many directions. Compared to permanent harbour surveillance systems, the PDDS-X is a portable system that can be placed in different positions to provide surveillance of the area to be protected.
The system is reported to be able to be deployed from a ship or to be installed at a harbour, including around walls, piers and on the seabed. Underwater divers can represent a security threat, since traditional surface surveillance systems may not detect a submerged person approaching a vessel or exclusive maritime area.
A specific diver-detection sonar can provide an acoustic means of detecting these contacts before reaching the protected area.The PDDS-X thus complements traditional surface surveillance systems by providing an underwater surveillance capability. It is also stated that its portability could make it possible to change the location of the sonar depending on the requirements.
The development represents another indigenous effort to address underwater security requirements, particularly around ships, harbours and shallow-water areas where protection against covert underwater intrusion is required.
Edited by Raunak Kunde

articles.title: Sagar Defence Teases Autonomous Helicopter for Navy Ships
articles.text:
Pune-based Sagar Defence Engineering (SDE) seems to be teasing a new autonomous aerial vehicle meant to be operated from warships, possibly broadening their existing portfolio of unmanned maritime systems into the domain of ship-borne autonomous aviation.
The company has shared a teaser on social media showing an aerial platform, but one of the existing teaser does not offer enough information to say whether it is an aircraft, its propulsion system, size or mission. Sagar Defence has yet to publicly confirmed the aircraft is autonomous helicopter. SDE has previously made unmanned surface and underwater vehicles and had been linked with autonomous systems for maritime and defence missions.
The company says its systems have built-in autonomous navigation, collision avoidance, communications and other control features. It has also previously worked on Varuna an unmanned personal aerial vehicle manufactured for the navy under its iDEX-Sprint initiative.
The Talwar An Indian Navy Free-fall Penetrator (INGR) drone developed by DRDO programme identifier DRDO More recently Sagar Defence has been talking about the difficult engineering challenge of autonomous take-off and landing from moving ships. It has specifically referred to ship-based drone operations and its Spotters concept, pointing to the challenge of using autonomous ships across the vessel’s Yaw, speed, sway, surge, pitches and rolls. If the teaser does indeed represent a helicopter-type aircraft, it could have benefits over fixed-wing types when operating from ships.
There are no runway requirements for a VTOL platform, and it could be fitted to the decks of frigates, destroyers or larger support ships depending on the aircraft size and deck handling needs.
Naval uses may involve observation, tracking of targets, communications relay or persistent Surveillance, reconnaissance and tracking of targets. These are yet to be officially confirmed capabilities of the electronic teaser.
The system was revealed days after the news broke that Sagar Defence received a government industrial licence authorising the manufacture of specified surface and underwater vessels and related military systems and platforms for design, construction, integration, assembly, testing and supply in export as well as domestic markets, subject to conditions and approvals. SDE has not announced the aircraft platform’s given name, endurance, payload, powerplant, level of independence or if the platform has flown from a ship.

While potentially useful, they can do real damage if not used carefully.

He said/she said

Meta CTO David Singleton joined the fray with a rebuttal that appeared solid. For Muse to access Apple Messages, a user must manually give it two privileges. One is full-disk access, a macOS system-level permission. The other is to enable a Messages connector setting in Muse.
